Wednesday, 11:40 p.m.
Same as Tuesday. Same as Monday. Bus at 8:12, same seat, same man eating the same banana. Twelve invoices, a meeting that could've been an email, lunch at my desk. Bus home.
I'm not sad. I checked. It's more like everything's gone grey and a bit heavy, like a sweater left out in the rain.
Got home, ate, and then scrolled for three hours. I don't remember a single thing I saw. Gopika messaged about the pottery class she keeps talking about. I left it on read. It felt like too much effort, which is ridiculous, because scrolling is also effort, just the kind that goes nowhere.
Tomorrow I'll reply to her. Probably.
— Sangeeta

passage: Every morning Harsha took the 9:05 bus from Hassan to the bank branch in Holenarasipur. Every morning the same fields, the same broken milestone, the same tea stall where he bought the same half-cup. At the counter: passbooks, withdrawal slips, the fan ticking overhead. He wasn't unhappy. He just felt grey, as if the colour had been washed out of the day. Evenings, he lay on his rented cot playing the same phone game until midnight, level after level, not really caring if he won. Gargi from the loans desk had asked twice if he'd join the Sunday cycling group to the lake. Twice he'd said, 'Next week.' Tonight he reached level 400. He felt nothing at all. He put the phone down and stared at the ceiling.

Every weekday, Rafael took the 7:48 metro from Amadora into Lisbon, stood in the same corner of the same carriage, and reached the insurance office at 8:30. Claims forms, the same eleven questions, lunch at his desk. He wasn't unhappy. He was grey, the way the river looks under cloud.
At home he put on a series, not really watching, and scrolled his phone through it, then ordered food he didn't feel like eating. Some nights it was two in the morning before he noticed.
His flatmate Javier knocked one Thursday. "Climbing gym tomorrow? You used to love it."
Rafael looked at the ceiling. "Maybe next week."
He said the same the following Thursday. The series kept playing. He couldn't have told you what it was about.

The medical records office in the hospital basement had no windows. Ritu, twenty-five, sat at desk four and coded the same kinds of discharge files she had coded for two years: date, ward, code, save, next. By eleven she was on autopilot. By three she had the shopping app open under the spreadsheet, filling a cart with things she didn't want and never bought. At four she bought chips from the vending machine without being hungry.
Zubin, at desk five, leaned back. "They're forming a volunteer team for the health camp next month. Want to sign up?"
Ritu shrugged. "Maybe."
She didn't sign up. At six she walked to the bus on the same path, and at home she opened the same app. Nothing was wrong. Everything was the same grey.

qa.a: Chips, without being hungry.

qa.a: It suggests she's numbing the dull sameness of her days rather than wanting anything in particular.

qa.a: Zubin's invitation to the health camp team; it could have brought new people and purpose into her grey routine.

passage:
Deepika, you asked why I push you juniors to take the weekend workshops. Let me tell you about the year I was twenty-five.
I was at a bank branch in Nagpur. Same counter, same forms, same bus at 8:40. Not unhappy. Just grey. Like living inside an old photograph.
Every evening I would come home, sit in front of the TV and eat a whole packet of namkeen. I didn't even enjoy the programmes. On Sundays I slept till noon so the day would be shorter.
Two years went like that. Two years I can barely remember.
Then my colleague Rehana dragged me to a Sunday Kannada class, of all things. I went only so she'd stop asking. And I remember walking out that first day feeling awake for the first time in months.
I'm Swati, and I think about those two lost years every time I see a junior go grey.

qa.q: Where did Swati work when she was twenty-five?
qa.a: At a bank branch in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling during those two years?
qa.a: Swati felt grey and dull, not unhappy but numb, going through the days without enjoying them.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Swati's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Going to the Sunday Kannada class with Rehana was the turning point, because trying something new broke the grey routine.

qa.q: How might Rehana have seen Swati during those years?
qa.a: Rehana probably noticed Swati seemed flat and stuck, and kept asking because she cared.

The monsoon had turned the Kochi bypass into a slow river of honking cars, and Jomon's bus had been stuck for forty minutes. He didn't look out of the window. He played the same puzzle game on his phone, level after level, not really seeing it.
IT support, year three. Same tickets, same passwords reset, same jokes in the pantry. He wasn't sad. He was just tired of the sameness, tired in a way sleep didn't fix.
His sister Farida called. "Coming for lunch Sunday?"
"Maybe. Tired."
"You always say tired."
He did. On Sundays he stayed in bed with the curtains shut and videos playing, one after another.
The bus lurched forward. He moved to the next level. It was easier than thinking about what he actually wanted.

passage:
I'm Rajni, and looking back at my second year at the bank, I can see how grey I had gone. The same 9:10 train, the same counter, the same forms, the same chai from the same stall. I wasn't unhappy. I just stopped noticing anything.
The weekends were the strange part: I'd sleep till noon, then fill carts on shopping apps at midnight and delete them in the morning. It gave me a tiny buzz and nothing else. When Arohi asked what I wanted to do on my birthday, I said, "Nothing, honestly." She stared at me. "You used to plan trips for months." I laughed it off.
I didn't change anything that year. I just kept filling and emptying carts.

Same bus. Same 8:12 from the depot. Same spreadsheet. Same lunch, rajma-rice from the canteen, because choosing takes effort. Same bus back. I'm not unhappy. That's the weird part. Nothing is wrong. It's just grey. Tonight I ate a whole packet of chips in front of the TV and watched four episodes of something I won't remember tomorrow. I think I'm scared that if I change anything, I'll notice how tired I am of all of it. Easier to just scroll. I don't love writing that down.

Parveen

Her cousin Sunaina knocked that evening. "Come and help us paint the ghat steps, na? It'll be fun."

After Sunaina left, she lay on the cot with her phone, thumb flicking through short videos she would not remember, until the screen said 1:12 a.m.
